title: G1124 — Writing, Holy Writ, and Scripture
body:
> **Movement III — What Is the Bible?**

---

## Chapter Assignment

Chapter 20 established the lexical and biblical significance of **γραφή (*graphē*)**, Strong's G1124. It established that the word belongs fundamentally to the field of writing and what is written, while biblical usage gives it the distinctive sense of Scripture or Holy Writ.

Chapter 21 now develops the next necessary question:

> **How does a writing come to be designated Holy Writ, and how does biblical usage identify authoritative written material as Scripture?**

The chapter therefore moves from the lexical identity of *graphē* to the biblical category of **holy writings and authoritative Scripture**.

The purpose is not to collapse every written document into Scripture, nor to begin the later investigation of canon before its proper place.

The purpose is to establish the biblical distinction between:

- writing in general;
- holy writings;
- Scripture;
- particular Scriptural passages;
- and the authoritative written testimony recognized in the biblical record.

---

## Central Objective

> **To establish from the biblical record and relevant lexical evidence why Scripture is distinguished from writing in general, how the category of Holy Writ is expressed, and how authoritative written material is identified as Scripture.**

---

# 21.1 Writing Is a Broad Category

Chapter 20 established that *graphē* belongs to the field of writing and what is written.

That immediately gives us an essential distinction:

> **Not everything that is written is Scripture.**

The Bible itself contains many kinds of writing.

There are:

- historical records;
- genealogies;
- laws;
- songs;
- letters;
- prophetic writings;
- personal communications;
- royal records;
- and other forms of written material.

Therefore the existence of writing does not by itself establish the existence of Scripture.

The question is more precise:

> **What distinguishes the writings that are Holy Writ?**

That question is necessary because the biblical category of Scripture is narrower than the generic category of written material.

---

# 21.2 Holy Writings — ἱερὰ γράμματα

Paul gives us an important starting point in 2 Timothy 3:15:

> **“And that from a child thou hast known the holy scriptures...”**

The Greek expression is:

> **ἱερὰ γράμματα**  
> *hiera grammata*

The noun **γράμματα (*grammata*)** belongs to the field of letters, writings, or written material.

The adjective **ἱερά (*hiera*)** identifies something as holy or sacred.

Paul therefore describes the writings Timothy has known as:

> **holy writings.**

This is already more precise than the generic category of writing.

The text does not merely say:

> “you have known writings.”

It identifies a particular body of writings as **holy**.

---

# 21.3 The Holy Writings Were Known

Paul says Timothy had known these holy writings:

> **“from a child.”**

The statement places the sacred writings within an existing historical and educational context.

Timothy had encountered them before Paul's letter.

They were not being created by Paul's statement.

They were an already existing body of sacred writings known to Timothy.

Paul then identifies their function:

> **“which are able to make thee wise unto salvation through faith which is in Christ Jesus.”**

The writings therefore possess a specific theological function.

They communicate knowledge capable of making Timothy wise unto salvation.

The significance is substantial:

> **Holy Writ is not merely writing distinguished by age or religious interest; it is sacred written testimony possessing a defined divine purpose.**

---

# 21.4 Holy Writ and Scripture

Paul immediately continues:

> **“All scripture is given by inspiration of God, and is profitable...”**

The Greek text uses:

> **πᾶσα γραφή**  
> *pasa graphē*

The relationship between verses 15 and 16 is therefore central.

Verse 15:

> **ἱερὰ γράμματα — holy writings**

Verse 16:

> **πᾶσα γραφή — all Scripture**

The terms are not identical.

That distinction must be preserved.

Yet they occur in immediate literary connection.

Paul has just described Timothy's sacred writings and then speaks of *graphē* in the statement concerning Scripture.

The passage therefore gives us an important biblical bridge between:

> **holy writings**

and:

> **Scripture.**

The detailed doctrine of **θεόπνευστος (*theopneustos*)**, and the scope of “all Scripture,” will be developed in their designated later chapters.

Here the relevant conclusion is:

> **The biblical record distinguishes sacred written material and identifies Scripture as a specific category of written testimony.**

---

# 21.5 Sacred Status Is Not Created by Human Preference

The biblical category of Holy Writ is not presented as a matter of personal preference.

A writing does not become Scripture because:

- someone likes it;
- a community finds it inspiring;
- a ruler approves it;
- it becomes popular;
- or generations happen to preserve it.

The biblical record presents Scripture as possessing a status grounded in its relationship to God's revelation.

This is why the question of **origin** remains important.

Chapter 19 examined the Bible's own claims concerning divine communication and origin.

Chapter 21 now sees the consequence in the written category:

> **A written testimony can be treated as Holy Writ because of what it is and the authority it bears, not merely because it is a surviving ancient document.**

---

# 21.6 Scripture as Authoritative Written Testimony

The biblical treatment of Scripture demonstrates its authority repeatedly.

Jesus asks:

> **“Have ye not read in the scriptures?”**

(Matthew 21:42).

He says:

> **“Ye do err, not knowing the scriptures”**

(Matthew 22:29).

He tells His hearers:

> **“Search the scriptures”**

(John 5:39).

The apostles reason from:

> **“the scriptures”**

(Acts 17:2).

The Bereans search:

> **“the scriptures daily”**

(Acts 17:11).

These passages reveal an established category.

Scripture is not treated as ordinary literature whose relevance must first be invented by the reader.

It is already recognized as authoritative written testimony.

---

# 21.7 Scripture as a Standard for Examination

Acts 17:11 is especially important.

The Bereans receive Paul's message with readiness of mind, but they do not stop with hearing.

They examine the Scriptures:

> **“whether those things were so.”**

This establishes a significant relationship between:

> **apostolic proclamation**

and:

> **written Scripture.**

The written Scripture functions as a standard against which the proclamation can be examined.

This is not hostility to revelation.

It is the biblical model of disciplined examination.

The sequence is:

> **hearing → examining → comparing → determining.**

The existence of an authoritative written standard makes such examination possible.

---

# 21.8 Jesus' Use of Scripture

Jesus repeatedly appeals to Scripture in His own teaching.

During His temptation, He answers Satan with:

> **“It is written”**

(Matthew 4:4, 7, 10).

In Matthew 21:42, He appeals to Psalm 118.

In Matthew 22:31–32, He appeals to the Scriptures concerning the resurrection.

In John 10:34–36, He appeals to Psalm 82:6 and explicitly states:

> **“the scripture cannot be broken.”**

In Luke 24:27, He explains what was written concerning Himself from Moses and all the Prophets.

In Luke 24:44–46, He connects His death and resurrection with what was written in:

- the Law of Moses;
- the Prophets;
- and the Psalms.

The pattern is consistent.

Scripture functions as authoritative written testimony.

---

# 21.9 “The Scripture Cannot Be Broken”

John 10:34–36 deserves particular attention.

Jesus cites Psalm 82:6:

> **“I said, Ye are gods.”**

His argument depends upon the written wording.

He then says:

> **“the scripture cannot be broken.”**

The statement occurs within an argument, not as an isolated slogan.

Jesus is appealing to a written text whose authority constrains the argument being made against Him.

The conclusion relevant here is:

> **Jesus treats the Scriptural text as authoritative and binding within theological reasoning.**

The full implications of Scriptural authority belong to later development.

But the evidence establishes that Scripture is not being treated as ordinary writing.

---

# 21.10 Scripture and Fulfillment

Another defining feature of Scripture is its relationship to fulfillment.

The Gospel writers repeatedly introduce events with language such as:

> **“that the scripture might be fulfilled.”**

This is particularly prominent in the accounts of Christ's ministry, suffering, death, and resurrection.

The written Scripture therefore functions as a prior testimony against which later historical events can be understood.

The pattern is:

> **written testimony → historical occurrence → claimed fulfillment.**

The validity of any individual fulfillment claim requires examination of:

- the original passage;
- its literary context;
- its historical setting;
- the chronology;
- the nature of the prediction;
- the subsequent event;
- and the correspondence between them.

But the category itself is clear.

Scripture is treated as written testimony that can bear authoritative witness concerning God's purposes in history.

---

# 21.11 Prophetic Writing and Scripture

The New Testament explicitly connects Scripture with the prophets.

Romans 16:26 speaks of:

> **“the scriptures of the prophets.”**

Matthew 26:56 similarly refers to:

> **“the scriptures of the prophets.”**

This establishes an important relationship.

A prophet may receive and speak a divine message.

That message may subsequently be written.

The written prophetic testimony can then become part of the Scriptural record.

Therefore:

> **Prophecy and Scripture are related categories, but they are not identical categories.**

Prophecy concerns prophetic communication.

Scripture concerns the authoritative written testimony.

This distinction will become essential in Movement IV, where the various ways God gave the written record are examined.

---

# 21.12 Scripture Can Preserve Earlier Revelation

The relationship between prophecy and Scripture reveals something broader.

The Bible preserves communications that originated earlier in history.

God speaks.

Prophets proclaim.

Events occur.

Writings preserve the testimony.

Later generations read those writings as Scripture.

Thus Scripture serves as a bridge across generations.

The original speaker may no longer be alive.

The original audience may have disappeared.

The political circumstances may have changed completely.

Yet the written testimony remains available.

This is one of the defining evidential characteristics of the written record.

---

# 21.13 Scripture as a Continuing Witness

A spoken testimony can be heard by those present.

A written testimony can continue to testify after the original speaker has died.

This is why Scripture repeatedly remains present as a witness to later generations.

Jesus can appeal to Moses.

The apostles can appeal to the Prophets.

Later Christians can read the same writings.

The historical distance does not erase the existence of the written testimony.

The writing preserves the witness.

Therefore:

> **The written Scripture functions as a continuing historical and theological witness across generations.**

This helps explain why the biblical writers repeatedly appeal to things that were:

> **“written.”**

---

# 21.14 The Authority of the Written Word

The Bible's treatment of Scripture demonstrates several dimensions of authority.

Scripture can:

- command;
- testify;
- correct;
- instruct;
- establish an argument;
- expose error;
- announce promises;
- record prophecy;
- bear witness to Christ;
- and provide a standard for examination.

The authority is therefore not merely ceremonial.

Scripture actually performs authoritative work in the biblical argument.

It is used to establish what is true, expose what is false, and interpret historical events.

---

# 21.15 Scripture and Christ

The relationship between Christ and Scripture is especially important.

Jesus does not present Himself as abolishing the Scriptures.

He says:

> **“Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets”**

(Matthew 5:17).

He repeatedly interprets His own mission through the written Scriptures.

After His resurrection, He teaches His disciples concerning:

> **“the things concerning himself.”**

Luke 24:27 describes Him beginning with Moses and all the Prophets and expounding the things concerning Himself in all the Scriptures.

The relationship is therefore profound:

> **Christ is not presented as an alternative to the authority of Scripture; He confirms and fulfills the Scriptural testimony concerning Himself.**

This becomes particularly important when the book later examines Christ as the decisive manifestation and communication of God.

---

# 21.16 Scripture and the Apostolic Witness

The apostles likewise appeal to Scripture as the written framework for their proclamation.

Paul summarizes the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4:

> **“Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures”**

and:

> **“he rose again the third day according to the scriptures.”**

The apostolic proclamation is therefore not presented as detached from the written testimony that preceded it.

The apostles proclaim historical events and interpret those events in relation to Scripture.

The structure is:

> **historical event + apostolic testimony + Scriptural correspondence.**

This connects the historical and evidential dimensions developed in Chapters 17 and 18 with the written category being examined here.

---

# 21.17 The Apostolic Writings and “the Other Scriptures”

A particularly important text is 2 Peter 3:15–16.

Peter refers to Paul's letters and then says that unstable people distort them:

> **“as they do also the other scriptures.”**

The phrase:

> **τὰς λοιπὰς γραφάς**

means:

> **“the other Scriptures.”**

The passage therefore places Paul's writings in a relationship with an already recognized Scriptural category.

This is significant internal evidence.

It does not by itself give the entire history of the New Testament canon.

But it does establish that, within the New Testament itself, apostolic writings could be spoken of in relation to:

> **the other Scriptures.**

That is an important development in the biblical evidence for the Scriptural category.

---

# 21.18 What 2 Peter 3:16 Establishes

The argument must remain precise.

Peter establishes that:

1. Paul wrote letters.
2. Some things in those letters are difficult to understand.
3. Unstable people distort those writings.
4. They do so in the same manner in which they distort:
   > **“the other scriptures.”**

The comparison is significant.

It means that Paul's writings are not being treated merely as private correspondence with no Scriptural standing.

At minimum, the passage provides strong internal evidence that apostolic writings were being placed within the recognized category of Scripture.

The complete question of the canonical corpus remains a later historical investigation.

But the textual evidence here belongs to the present argument.

---

# 21.19 Scripture Is Not Created by the Canonical List

Another distinction is necessary.

A writing does not become Scripture merely because a later list contains its name.

The historical recognition of a writing and the underlying identity of the writing are related but distinct questions.

The Bible's own language concerns writings already functioning as sacred and authoritative testimony.

The later historical question is:

> **How were the writings belonging to that category identified, received, preserved, and recognized?**

That is the question of canon.

Therefore:

> **Scripture must first be understood as a category before the historical process of recognizing the canonical corpus can be fully examined.**

---

# 21.20 Holy Writ Is Not the Same as Religious Literature

The category of Holy Writ is more precise than:

> **religious literature.**

Religious literature can include:

- theological reflections;
- sermons;
- devotional works;
- historical accounts;
- philosophical arguments;
- traditions;
- commentaries;
- confessions;
- and countless other writings.

These may discuss God, Scripture, faith, morality, or religion.

But they are not thereby Scripture.

The distinction is therefore essential:

> **Religious writing is a broad human category. Holy Writ is a specific Scriptural category.**

This is precisely why the Bible's own terminology must be examined rather than allowing modern categories to determine the argument.

---

# 21.21 Scripture and Human Authorship

The conclusion established in Chapter 19 remains fully operative.

Scripture comes to us through genuine human authorship.

Moses wrote.

The prophets wrote.

The psalmists wrote.

The Gospel writers wrote.

Paul wrote letters.

Peter wrote.

John wrote.

Yet some of these writings are identified as Scripture.

Therefore:

> **Human authorship does not prevent a writing from being Holy Writ.**

The biblical record does not require us to choose between:

> **divine origin**

and:

> **human authorship.**

The written Scripture comes through human literary activity while being presented as sacred and authoritative.

That is the historical form in which the written Word comes to humanity.

---

# 21.22 Scripture and Historical Particularity

Because the writings come through human authors, they possess historical particularity.

A writing has:

- a language;
- a historical setting;
- a literary form;
- an intended audience;
- a communicative purpose;
- and a historical context.

Understanding those features does not diminish Scriptural authority.

It enables accurate reading.

A prophetic oracle must be understood in its historical setting.

A Gospel narrative must be read according to its narrative and historical context.

An apostolic letter must be understood in relation to its recipients and circumstances.

Thus:

> **Historical context is not an enemy of Scripture; it is part of the evidence required to understand the Scripture correctly.**

---

# 21.23 Scripture as Written Testimony About Reality

The Bible's written Scriptures do not merely preserve theological abstractions.

They record claims concerning:

- persons;
- places;
- nations;
- kings;
- wars;
- covenants;
- births;
- deaths;
- journeys;
- judgments;
- promises;
- miracles;
- and historical events.

They therefore make claims that intersect with reality.

This is important because the book's investigation began with truth and reality.

If Scripture claims:

> **“this happened,”**

then the claim is capable of historical examination.

If Scripture claims:

> **“this was spoken,”**

the claim can be examined in relation to its historical and textual setting.

If Scripture claims:

> **“this was fulfilled,”**

the claimed correspondence can be examined.

Thus Holy Writ remains an evidentially accessible written record.

---

# 21.24 The Written Record Is Not Beyond Examination

The authority of Scripture does not make examination meaningless.

The Bereans examined.

The apostles reasoned.

Jesus argued from Scripture.

The biblical writers interpreted earlier written testimony.

Therefore the proper response to Scripture includes:

- reading;
- examination;
- comparison;
- interpretation;
- reasoning;
- and obedience.

This is consistent with the intellectual architecture established from Chapter 1 onward.

Truth is not established by repetition.

Knowledge is not reduced to quotation.

Scripture is not reduced to isolated proof texts.

And authority is not a substitute for understanding.

The Bible itself models serious engagement with the written Word.

---

# 21.25 The Distinction Between Scripture and Interpretation

A final methodological distinction is essential.

There is:

> **what Scripture says**

and:

> **what a person says Scripture means.**

Those are not automatically identical.

The biblical text is the primary object.

A commentary is a secondary witness.

A theological system is an interpretive construction.

A sermon is an exposition.

A study Bible contains editorial judgments.

A lexicon provides lexical information.

The manuscript must therefore preserve the distinction between:

> **Scripture**

and:

> **human commentary about Scripture.**

This principle is fundamental to the Doctrine of the Graphē.

---

# 21.26 The Cumulative Biblical Picture

The evidence can now be assembled.

### First

Writing is a broad category.

### Second

The Bible identifies a category of **holy writings**.

### Third

The New Testament uses **γραφή** as a designation for Scripture.

### Fourth

Jesus and the apostles treat Scripture as authoritative.

### Fifth

Scripture is used as a standard for examining claims.

### Sixth

Scripture bears witness to God's purposes and historical fulfillment.

### Seventh

Prophetic writings can function as Scripture.

### Eighth

The New Testament provides evidence that apostolic writings could be included within the Scriptural category.

The conclusion is therefore not based on one isolated verse.

It arises from the cumulative pattern.

---

# 21.27 The Argumentative Chain

>

>
> **The Bible contains many kinds of writing**

---

# 21.28 What This Chapter Establishes

This chapter has established:

1. **Writing is broader than Scripture.**
2. **The Bible identifies a category of “holy writings.”**
3. **2 Timothy 3:15–16 provides a direct textual relationship between holy writings and Scripture.**
4. **γραφή is used for Scripture within the New Testament.**
5. **Jesus treats Scripture as authoritative written testimony.**
6. **The apostles likewise reason from and appeal to Scripture.**
7. **Scripture functions as a standard for examining claims.**
8. **Scripture preserves prophetic testimony and bears witness to God's purposes in history.**
9. **Scripture is treated as a continuing witness across generations.**
10. **2 Peter 3:16 provides internal evidence concerning apostolic writings and the Scriptural category.**
11. **Holy Writ is distinct from religious literature generally.**
12. **Human authorship does not prevent a writing from being Scripture.**
13. **Scriptural identity and the later historical recognition of the canonical corpus are related but distinct questions.**
14. **The written Scripture is the authoritative written category at the center of the present investigation.**

---

# 21.29 What This Chapter Has Not Yet Attempted

This chapter has not attempted to:

- provide the complete doctrine of inspiration;
- enumerate the complete biblical canon;
- reconstruct the entire history of canonical recognition;
- establish every question concerning textual preservation;
- examine every mode through which God communicated;
- or complete the final apologetic argument for biblical authority.

Those questions have their proper places.

The present chapter has established the category itself:

> **Holy Writ is sacred and authoritative written testimony, and γραφή is a principal biblical designation for Scripture.**

---

# 21.30 Transition to Chapter 22

The investigation has now moved through three increasingly precise categories:

> **writing**

→

> **holy writings**

→

> **Scripture / γραφή.**

But the Bible and Christian tradition employ several related designations:

- Graphē;
- Holy Writ;
- Scripture;
- the Scriptures;
- the Bible;
- the written Word;
- and related expressions.

These terms are closely connected, but they should not simply be treated as interchangeable without examination.

The next chapter will therefore establish their relationship.

> **What is the relationship among Graphē, Holy Writ, Scripture, Bible, and Written Word—and what exactly is the written authority being investigated?**

That is the task of Chapter 22.

---

# Lexical and Evidence Notes

## γραφή (*graphē*) — G1124

The lexical field of **γραφή** concerns writing or what is written. In New Testament usage, the term is repeatedly used for Scripture or Holy Writ and can also designate a particular Scriptural passage.

The lexical meaning must not be expanded into a claim that every occurrence of γραφή means “the Bible.” Context determines the scope.

## γράμματα (*grammata*)

In 2 Timothy 3:15, Paul speaks of:

> **ἱερὰ γράμματα**

holy writings.

The expression is significant because it provides a direct biblical description of sacred written material immediately before the statement concerning:

> **πᾶσα γραφή**

all/every Scripture.

## 2 Peter 3:16

Peter's description of Paul's letters alongside:

> **“the other scriptures”**

provides important internal evidence concerning apostolic writings and the Scriptural category.

The passage should be used for what it actually establishes, without making it carry the entire later history of canonical recognition.

---

# Chapter's Central Conclusion

> **The Bible distinguishes ordinary writing from Holy Writ: Scripture is sacred and authoritative written testimony, identified within the biblical record as γραφή (*graphē*), and human authorship is the historical means through which this written testimony has been communicated and preserved.**

---

## Chapter Assignment

The preceding chapters have progressively identified the object under investigation.

Chapter 16 established the Bible as a **divine library and written record**.

Chapter 17 examined the Bible as **historical testimony**.

Chapter 18 examined its **eyewitness and apostolic testimony**.

Chapter 19 gathered the Bible's own claims concerning its **origin, divine communication, inspiration, prophetic speech, apostolic testimony, and Scripture**.

Chapter 20 introduced **γραφή (*graphē*)**, Strong's G1124.

Chapter 21 developed the relationship between **writing, Holy Writ, and Scripture**.

Chapter 22 now asks a necessary terminological question:

> **How do Graphē, Holy Writ, Scripture, the Scriptures, the Bible, and the Written Word relate to one another?**

The purpose is not to flatten these expressions into interchangeable synonyms.

Neither is it to manufacture distinctions where the biblical and historical evidence shows substantial overlap.

The purpose is precision.

Before the investigation proceeds to **how the written record was given**, the reader must know exactly what is meant by the written authority under investigation.

---

# Central Objective

> **To establish the precise relationship among Graphē, Holy Writ, Scripture, the Scriptures, the Bible, and the Written Word, distinguishing their lexical origins, biblical usage, historical development, and conceptual functions while establishing the authoritative written corpus that is the object of the investigation.**

The chapter therefore moves through four tasks:

1. **Define the principal terms.**
2. **Distinguish their respective functions.**
3. **Show where their meanings overlap.**
4. **Establish precisely what is meant by the biblical written authority being investigated.**

---

# 22.1 Why Terminology Matters

An investigation cannot remain precise if the object being investigated is allowed to change meaning from one paragraph to another.

Consider the following expressions:

- writing;
- Holy Writ;
- Scripture;
- the Scriptures;
- Bible;
- Word of God;
- Written Word;
- God's Word.

These expressions are closely related.

But they are not all formed from the same word, do not all have the same lexical history, and do not always have the same referent in every biblical context.

That does not weaken their relationship.

It clarifies it.

The governing principle is therefore:

> **Where terms overlap, establish the overlap. Where they differ, preserve the distinction.**

This prevents two opposite errors.

### Error 1 — Flattening

Treating every expression as though it were linguistically identical.

### Error 2 — Fragmenting

Treating closely related expressions as though they referred to unrelated realities.

The correct method is to determine the relationship from the evidence.

---

# 22.2 The First Distinction: Writing Is Broader Than Scripture

Chapter 20 established the basic lexical field of **γραφή (*graphē*)**.

Writing is a broad human activity.

People write:

- histories;
- letters;
- laws;
- records;
- poems;
- contracts;
- genealogies;
- reports;
- personal correspondence;
- inscriptions;
- administrative documents;
- and many other forms of communication.

Therefore:

> **Writing by itself does not mean Scripture.**

This is an elementary distinction, but it is foundational.

The Bible itself contains different kinds of written material.

The question is not:

> “Is it written?”

The more precise question is:

> **“What kind of writing is it, and what authority does it possess?”**

The biblical category of Scripture is therefore more specific than the generic category of writing.

---

# 22.3 Graphē — γραφή

The Greek noun:

> **γραφή (*graphē*)**

is derived from the verbal field associated with writing.

Its fundamental lexical sense concerns:

> **writing, a writing, or what has been written.**

In the New Testament, however, *graphē* acquires a highly significant specialized usage.

It is repeatedly used for:

> **Scripture / Holy Writ.**

This is why the word must be understood at two levels.

### Lexical level

> **γραφή — writing / what is written.**

### Biblical usage

> **γραφή — Scripture, the sacred written text.**

The second meaning is not an arbitrary invention.

It arises from the repeated way the New Testament uses the word in its Scriptural context.

---

# 22.4 Singular and Plural Scripture

The New Testament uses both singular and plural forms.

A singular expression can identify:

> **a particular Scripture or written passage.**

A plural expression can identify:

> **the Scriptures as a body of sacred writings.**

This distinction is visible in passages such as Matthew 21:42 and Mark 12:10.

Jesus can ask:

> **“Have ye not read in the scriptures...?”**

while a particular passage can be identified as:

> **“this scripture.”**

Therefore the word *graphē* can function both for:

- a particular Scriptural text;
- and the broader Scriptural corpus.

The context determines the scope.

This is why it is inaccurate to say that *graphē* mechanically means “the complete Bible” every time it appears.

Its biblical usage is richer and more precise.

---

# 22.5 Holy Writ — ἱερὰ γράμματα

2 Timothy 3:15 provides another important designation:

> **ἱερὰ γράμματα (*hiera grammata*)**

commonly rendered:

> **“holy scriptures,”**
>
> **“sacred writings,”**
>
> or
>
> **“holy writings.”**

The expression contains two significant elements.

### ἱερά (*hiera*)

This identifies the writings as:

> **holy / sacred.**

### γράμματα (*grammata*)

This belongs to the field of:

> **letters, writings, written material.**

The combined expression therefore identifies:

> **sacred or holy writings.**

Paul then immediately speaks of:

> **πᾶσα γραφή (*pasa graphē*)**

in verse 16.

The literary connection is significant.

The passage therefore gives us two closely related designations:

> **holy writings**

and:

> **Scripture.**

The distinction in terminology should be preserved while the close relationship should also be recognized.

---

# 22.6 Holy Writ Is a Category of Sacred Writing

The adjective **holy** matters.

The Bible does not simply identify a collection of old writings.

It identifies sacred writings as belonging to a distinct category.

This means that the biblical question is not merely:

> “Is this document ancient?”

Nor:

> “Was this document written by a religious person?”

Nor:

> “Has this document been preserved?”

The more fundamental question is:

> **Does this writing belong to the category of Holy Writ?**

That question leads naturally into the biblical concept of Scripture.

---

# 22.7 Scripture — The English Designation

The English word **Scripture** corresponds to the biblical concept expressed principally by the Greek **γραφή** in New Testament usage.

The English term therefore carries the idea of:

> **sacred writing / Holy Writ.**

This is why expressions such as:

> **“the Scripture”**

and:

> **“the Scriptures”**

refer not simply to any written document but to the sacred written testimony recognized in the biblical record.

The word “Scripture” is therefore a designation of **status and function**, not merely physical form.

A document can be physically written without being Scripture.

Scripture is written testimony possessing a sacred and authoritative identity.

---

# 22.8 “The Scriptures”

The plural expression:

> **“the Scriptures”**

is particularly important.

Jesus and the apostles repeatedly appeal to:

> **“the Scriptures.”**

Examples include:

- Matthew 21:42;
- Matthew 22:29;
- Mark 12:24;
- Luke 24:27;
- John 5:39;
- Acts 17:11;
- Romans 15:4;
- 2 Peter 3:16.

The expression therefore functions as a recognized designation for a body of sacred writings.

This is important for understanding the Bible as a corpus.

The Bible is not presented as a single human composition written at one time.

It is a collection of writings that came through different authors, periods, circumstances, and literary forms.

The term **“the Scriptures”** naturally accommodates that plurality.

---

# 22.9 “It Is Written”

One of the most important Scriptural formulas is:

> **“It is written.”**

Jesus repeatedly uses this expression.

Examples include Matthew 4:4, 7, and 10.

The formula does something more than identify the existence of writing.

It appeals to the written text as an authoritative witness.

The reasoning is:

> **What has been written in Scripture carries authority in the present argument.**

This is why Jesus can answer temptation by appealing to what is written.

The written text is not merely an historical artifact.

It remains authoritative testimony.

---

# 22.10 Scripture as an Authoritative Written Witness

The cumulative biblical pattern is therefore clear.

Scripture is:

- read;
- searched;
- quoted;
- interpreted;
- fulfilled;
- appealed to;
- reasoned from;
- and treated as authoritative.

The Bereans examine Paul's preaching in relation to the Scriptures:

> **“whether those things were so.”**

Jesus argues from Scripture.

The apostles argue from Scripture.

Prophetic fulfillment is explained from Scripture.

The written text therefore functions as a continuing witness.

This is one of the most important characteristics of the written record.

---

# 22.11 The Bible — What Does the Name Mean?

We now come to the word:

> **Bible.**

The English word **Bible** is not the original biblical name for the collection.

It comes through Latin and related Western-language development from the Greek:

> **βιβλία (*biblia*)**

meaning:

> **“books.”**

The underlying Greek vocabulary is associated with **βιβλίον (*biblion*)**, a book, scroll, or written document, and **βίβλος (*biblos*)**, a term associated historically with writing material and books.

The essential point is simple:

> **Bible originally carries the idea of “books.”**

This is fitting because the Bible is a collection of writings rather than a single continuous composition.

---

# 22.12 The Historical Development of “Bible”

The historical development of the designation is especially illuminating.

The Greek expression:

> **τὰ βιβλία (*ta biblia*)**

means:

> **“the books.”**

The expression occurs in the Greek Old Testament tradition, including Daniel 9:2, where Daniel speaks of the books in connection with the prophetic writings.

The designation subsequently became associated with the sacred books of the Christian Scriptures.

The historical development then moved through several stages.

### Stage 1 — Books

The sacred writings were understood as:

> **the books.**

### Stage 2 — The Sacred Collection

Christian usage increasingly applied the designation to the corpus of sacred writings.

### Stage 3 — The Divine Library

Jerome, in the fourth century, used the significant designation:

> **Bibliotheca Divina**

or:

> **“The Divine Library.”**

That expression captures something important.

The Bible is simultaneously:

> **a unified corpus**

and:

> **a library of individual writings.**

### Stage 4 — From “Books” to “Book”

Over time, the plural designation came to be treated in Western usage as a singular collective designation.

Thus:

> **The Books**

became:

> **The Book**

and ultimately:

> **the Bible.**

This historical development helps explain why the modern word can refer to the whole collection as one entity.

---

# 22.13 The Bible Is Both “The Book” and “The Books”

This development does not erase the plurality of the biblical writings.

It actually gives us a useful conceptual distinction.

The Bible is:

> **the Book**

as a unified corpus.

And it is:

> **the Books**

as a collection of individual writings.

This is not a contradiction.

A library can be considered:

- collectively;
- and book by book.

Likewise, the Bible can be examined as:

- one corpus;
- or its individual books.

The historical designation therefore reflects a genuine feature of the object.

---

# 22.14 Bible as Corpus

The Bible's corpus character is evident from its structure.

In the standard Protestant Christian arrangement, the Bible contains:

> **66 books**

comprising:

- **39 books of the Old Testament**;
- **27 books of the New Testament**.

These writings were produced across different historical periods and literary settings.

They were written through different human agents and in different linguistic environments.

The Old Testament is principally associated with Hebrew, with portions in Aramaic.

The New Testament is written in Koine Greek.

Thus the Bible is not one manuscript in the ordinary sense.

It is a corpus.

That is why the historical development from:

> **“books”**

to:

> **“the Book”**

is conceptually significant.

The unity of the corpus does not erase the plurality of its constituent writings.

---

# 22.15 The Bible and Its Original Languages

The terminology must also be distinguished from the languages in which the writings were originally composed.

The biblical corpus comes to us through:

- Hebrew;
- Aramaic;
- and Greek.

This means that the English word:

> **Bible**

is not itself the original-language name found throughout the biblical texts.

It is a later historical designation for the collection.

That distinction is important because it prevents the modern English title from being projected backward as though it were the original name used by every biblical writer.

---

# 22.16 Bible, Scripture, and Holy Writ Are Related but Not Identical Terms

We can now state the relationship more precisely.

### Graphē

Emphasizes:

> **writing / what is written**

and in New Testament usage frequently:

> **Scripture.**

### Holy Writ

Emphasizes:

> **the sacred character of the writings.**

### Scripture

Emphasizes:

> **the authoritative sacred written testimony.**

### The Scriptures

Emphasizes:

> **the recognized body of sacred writings.**

### Bible

Historically emphasizes:

> **the collection of books as a corpus.**

These are not competing definitions.

They are different linguistic windows onto closely related aspects of the same written corpus.

---

# 22.17 The “Written Word”

The expression:

> **“Written Word”**

is a useful descriptive designation for God's Word in written form.

It should not be confused with the lexical meaning of *graphē* itself.

Nor should it be confused with every biblical use of:

> **λόγος (*logos*)**

or:

> **Word of God.**

The phrase “Written Word” emphasizes the form in which divine communication has been recorded and preserved:

> **written.**

Thus:

> **God's Word**
>
> ↓
>
> **communicated**
>
> ↓
>
> **received and witnessed**
>
> ↓
>
> **written**
>
> ↓
>
> **preserved as Scripture**

This relationship will become central in Movement IV.

---

# 22.18 “The Word of God” Is Broader Than One Technical Term

The expression:

> **“Word of God”**

must be handled with contextual precision.

In Scripture, God's Word can refer to:

- God's command;
- God's spoken declaration;
- prophetic proclamation;
- divine revelation;
- apostolic proclamation;
- Christ as the Word;
- and God's revealed message in written Scripture.

Therefore the expression should not be reduced mechanically to:

> **“the Bible.”**

At the same time, this distinction does not weaken the relationship between Scripture and God's Word.

The written Scriptures are presented as God's authoritative written testimony.

The correct conclusion is therefore:

> **“Word of God” is a broader biblical category whose particular referent is determined by context, while Scripture is the authoritative written category within that broader field.**

---

# 22.19 Christ as the Word and Scripture as Written Testimony

John 1:1 identifies Christ as:

> **ὁ λόγος — the Word.**

John 1:14 declares:

> **“the Word was made flesh.”**

This is fundamentally different from saying:

> “the Bible became flesh.”

Christ is personally the Word.

Scripture is written testimony.

The distinction must remain absolute.

Yet the relationship is profound.

God communicates Himself and His truth through multiple forms of divine communication.

The Bible records that communication.

Therefore the investigation must distinguish:

> **the divine Person**

from:

> **the divine message**

from:

> **the written testimony preserving that message.**

This distinction prevents confusion while allowing the full unity of divine revelation to be seen.

---

# 22.20 Scripture and the Written Record

The written record is therefore not identical with every event or every spoken word that occurred in biblical history.

It is the preserved written testimony.

For example:

> a prophet may receive a divine message;

> the prophet may proclaim it;

> the message may be witnessed;

> the message may be written;

> the written text may then be preserved;

> and the resulting writing may function as Scripture.

The written record is therefore a historically mediated form of divine communication.

That fact does not make it less significant.

It explains how revelation becomes accessible across generations.

---

# 22.21 Scripture Can Outlive Its First Audience

A spoken message is immediately available to those who hear it.

A written testimony can remain available long after the original audience has disappeared.

This is one reason the written record is so important.

Moses can be read by generations who never met Moses.

David's writings can be read by generations who never lived in David's court.

The prophets can be read by people centuries after their ministries.

The apostles can be read by people who were never present in Jerusalem, Galilee, Corinth, Ephesus, or Patmos.

The writing carries the testimony across time.

Thus:

> **The written form of Scripture makes the testimony historically transmissible across generations.**

---

# 22.22 Scripture, Manuscript, and Copy Must Be Distinguished

Another distinction is essential.

A **manuscript** is a physical written witness.

A **copy** is a reproduction of an earlier textual witness.

A **translation** renders the text into another language.

An **edition** presents a textual form according to editorial decisions.

A **Scriptural writing** is the authoritative sacred text belonging to the Scriptural corpus.

These categories are related but not identical.

This distinction will later become essential when the investigation turns to:

- manuscript evidence;
- textual transmission;
- copying;
- textual variants;
- preservation;
- and the history of the biblical text.

For now, the conclusion is sufficient:

> **The physical artifact carrying Scripture must not be confused with Scripture as the written textual authority.**

---

# 22.23 Scripture and Commentary Must Be Distinguished

The same principle applies to interpretation.

There is a fundamental difference between:

> **Scripture**

and:

> **a commentary on Scripture.**

There is a difference between:

> **the biblical text**

and:

> **a theological explanation of the biblical text.**

There is a difference between:

> **what the text says**

and:

> **what an interpreter concludes that it means.**

This distinction is necessary because the Doctrine of the Graphē is concerned first with the primary written testimony.

Secondary interpretation may be useful.

But it cannot silently replace the primary source.

The governing methodological rule remains:

> **What Scripture says must be distinguished from what someone says Scripture says.**

---

# 22.24 The Bible as a Library

The designation:

> **“The Divine Library”**

is therefore conceptually valuable.

A library contains:

- many books;
- different authors;
- different genres;
- different historical settings;
- and different subjects.

Yet the collection can still be treated as one library.

Likewise, the Bible contains diverse writings while forming one recognized corpus.

This is why:

> **diversity of authorship**

does not mean:

> **absence of corpus unity.**

And:

> **unity of corpus**

does not mean:

> **one human author.**

The distinction is fundamental to understanding the Bible as a written object.

---

# 22.25 The Bible's Unity Does Not Erase Its Diversity

The biblical corpus includes:

- law;
- narrative;
- poetry;
- wisdom;
- prophecy;
- Gospel narrative;
- apostolic history;
- letters;
- and apocalyptic literature.

The diversity is real.

The historical periods are real.

The human authors are real.

The languages are real.

The literary forms are real.

The individual books remain identifiable.

Yet these writings are received as one Scriptural corpus.

Therefore:

> **The Bible's unity must be understood as corpus unity, not as the denial of its literary and historical diversity.**

This observation will become increasingly important when later chapters examine inspiration and the means by which God gave the written record.

---

# 22.26 The Terminological Map

The relationship can now be summarized:

| Designation | Primary emphasis |
|---|---|
| **γραφή (*graphē*)** | Writing / what is written; frequently Scripture in New Testament usage |
| **ἱερὰ γράμματα (*hiera grammata*)** | Holy or sacred writings |
| **Scripture** | Sacred and authoritative written testimony |
| **The Scriptures** | The recognized body of sacred writings |
| **Bible** | The historical designation of the collected biblical books |
| **Written Word** | God's Word considered in its written form |
| **Word of God** | A broader biblical expression whose referent is determined by context |

This table should be read as a relationship map, not as a list of unrelated definitions.

---

# 22.27 What These Terms Have in Common

Although their emphases differ, the terms converge on the object now under investigation.

The Bible is the corpus.

The Scriptures are the sacred writings within that corpus.

Holy Writ emphasizes their sacred character.

Graphē identifies writing and, in biblical usage, Scripture.

Written Word emphasizes God's Word in written form.

Thus the investigation has arrived at a precise object:

> **the sacred and authoritative written corpus identified as Scripture and historically designated as the Bible.**

---

# 22.28 What These Terms Must Not Be Made to Mean

Precision also requires limits.

We should not say:

> **Every writing is Scripture.**

We should not say:

> **Every occurrence of γραφή means the entire Bible.**

We should not say:

> **Every occurrence of λόγος means the Bible.**

We should not say:

> **The physical manuscript is identical with the Scriptural authority it carries.**

We should not say:

> **A commentary is Scripture because it explains Scripture.**

We should not say:

> **The English word “Bible” was the original name used by all biblical writers.**

Each statement would confuse distinct categories.

---

# 22.29 Why “Bible” Is a Particularly Useful Name

The historical name “Bible” has an important conceptual strength.

Its original plural sense:

> **“books”**

reminds us that the Bible is not a single document produced in one sitting.

It is a collection.

It contains individual books.

Those books possess their own historical identities.

Yet they belong to a unified corpus.

The later singular use:

> **“the Book”**

emphasizes the unity of the collection.

Therefore the history of the name itself reflects an important feature of the object:

> **many writings, one recognized corpus.**

---

# 22.30 The Written Authority Being Investigated

We can now state the object of the investigation with precision.

The object is not:

- paper;
- ink;
- a particular printed edition;
- a modern translation;
- a commentary;
- a theological system;
- or a later author's explanation.

The object is:

> **the corpus of sacred writings identified as Scripture and historically collected and designated as the Bible.**

Its material witnesses are manuscripts.

Its individual components are books.

Its biblical designation is Scripture.

Its sacred character is expressed as Holy Writ.

Its written form may properly be described as the Written Word.

And its historical collective designation is:

> **the Bible.**

---

# 22.31 The Cumulative Argument

The investigation can now be expressed as a sequence.

> **Writing is a broad category**
>
> ↓
>
> **Some writings are identified as holy**
>
> ↓
>
> **Holy writings are identified as Scripture**
>
> ↓
>
> **γραφή becomes a principal New Testament designation for Scripture**
>
> ↓
>
> **“The Scriptures” identifies a body of sacred writings**
>
> ↓
>
> **The Bible historically comes from “the books”**
>
> ↓
>
> **The books form a corpus**
>
> ↓
>
> **The corpus is treated as one Scriptural collection**
>
> ↓
>
> **“Written Word” describes God's Word in its written form**
>
> ↓
>
> **The written authority under investigation is the Scriptural corpus historically designated as the Bible**

This is the necessary terminological foundation for the next movement.

---

# 22.32 The Bible Is a Collection — Not a Random Collection

The fact that the Bible consists of many books must not be misunderstood.

It is not simply a random shelf of ancient religious literature.

The writings belong to a recognized Scriptural corpus.

They have been transmitted as a body.

They are repeatedly treated within the biblical record as sacred written testimony.

The later historical questions concerning recognition, canon, transmission, and preservation are therefore not questions about whether unrelated books happened to be placed together.

They are questions concerning:

> **which writings belong to the Scriptural corpus and how that corpus was recognized and transmitted.**

Those questions have their proper place later in the investigation.

---

# 22.33 The Terminology Prepares the Next Question

The chapter has now answered:

> **What do we mean by the written authority?**

But another question immediately follows.

If Scripture is written testimony:

> **How did the written testimony come into existence?**

If the Bible is a corpus of sacred writings:

> **How were those writings given?**

If the Written Word is divine communication in written form:

> **How did divine communication become written testimony?**

That is not a question of terminology.

It is a question of origin and transmission.

And it is precisely the question assigned to the next movement.

---

# 22.34 Transition to Movement IV

The progression is now complete:

> **What is the Bible?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is Graphē?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is Holy Writ?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is Scripture?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is the Bible?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What is the Written Word?**
>
> ↓
>
> **What written authority are we investigating?**
>
> ↓
>
> **How was that written record given?**

The next movement therefore begins with the means by which divine communication entered the historical record.

The first mode is direct divine speech:

> **God speaking with an audible voice.**

Chapter 23 will therefore examine the biblical evidence for direct divine speech, including:

- Exodus 19:19;
- Deuteronomy 5;
- Matthew 3:16–17;
- John 12:28.

---

# 22.35 Chapter Conclusion

The terminology has now been placed in its proper relationship.

> **Graphē** identifies writing and, in its New Testament Scriptural usage, Scripture.

> **Holy Writ / holy writings** identifies sacred written material.

> **Scripture** identifies the authoritative sacred written testimony.

> **The Scriptures** identifies the recognized body of such writings.

> **Bible** is the historical designation that developed from the concept of “the books” and came to designate the collected biblical corpus.

> **Written Word** describes God's Word in its written form.

These expressions overlap because they converge upon the same Scriptural corpus, but they are not linguistically or conceptually identical.

The central conclusion is therefore:

> **The Bible is the collected corpus of sacred writings identified as Scripture; Graphē is a principal biblical designation for Scripture; Holy Writ emphasizes the sacred character of the writings; and “Written Word” describes God's Word in its written form. Together, these designations identify the written authority whose origin, transmission, authentication, and preservation the following movements will investigate.**

The terminological question has therefore been settled sufficiently to move forward.

The next question is no longer:

> **What are we talking about?**

It is:

> **How did God give the written record?**

---
